canonical_statement: Assess the medical, psychological, functional, including self-management abilities, and social domains in older adults with diabetes using a comprehensive approach to determine diabetes management goals and therapeutic approaches.
Screen older adults with diabetes at least annually for geriatric syndromes, hypoglycemia, and polypharmacy because these problems may affect diabetes management and diminish quality of life.
Screen adults 65 years of age or older for early mild cognitive impairment or dementia at the initial visit, annually, and as appropriate.
Ascertain and address hypoglycemia at routine visits because older adults with diabetes have greater hypoglycemia risk, especially when treated with sulfonylureas, meglitinides, or insulin.

Recommend continuous glucose monitoring for older adults with type 1 diabetes, source grade A, and for older adults with type 2 diabetes on insulin therapy, source grade B, to improve glycemic outcomes, reduce hypoglycemia, and reduce treatment burden.

Consider automated insulin delivery systems, source grade B, and other advanced insulin delivery devices such as connected pens, source grade E, to reduce hypoglycemia risk based on individual ability and support.

For older adults with few stable coexisting chronic illnesses and intact cognitive and functional status, use lower glycemic goals such as A1C below 7.0 to 7.5 percent and, when CGM is used, TIR 70 to 180 mg/dL of at least 70 percent and TBR at or below 70 mg/dL of at most 4 percent.

For older adults with intermediate or complex health, individualize glycemic goals and prioritize avoidance of hypoglycemia, using less stringent goals such as A1C below 8.0 percent and, when CGM is used, TIR 70 to 180 mg/dL of at least 50 percent and TBR below 70 mg/dL of less than 1 percent when cognitive or functional limitations, frailty, severe comorbidities, or an unfavorable medication risk-benefit ratio are present.
For older adults with very complex or poor health, focus on avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia because stringent glycemic goals provide minimal benefit.
Individualize screening for diabetes complications in older adults and prioritize complications that would impair functional status or quality of life.

For most older adults with diabetes, use an on-treatment blood pressure goal below 130/80 mmHg when it can be achieved safely, source grade A. A more relaxed goal such as below 140/90 mmHg may be used for poor health, limited life expectancy, or high risk of adverse effects, source grade E.

Individualize treatment of other cardiovascular risk factors in older adults by considering time to benefit. Lipid-lowering therapy and antiplatelet agents may benefit people whose life expectancy is at least as long as the time frame of the relevant prevention or intervention trials.

Recommend healthful eating with protein intake of at least 0.8 g/kg body weight per day for older adults with diabetes to maintain lean body mass, with higher individualized amounts when needed to regain lean body mass and function.

Recommend regular physical activity, including aerobic activity, weight-bearing exercise, and resistance training as tolerated for older adults who can safely participate, particularly to maintain lean body mass and especially during weight loss.

For older adults with type 2 diabetes, overweight or obesity, and capacity to exercise safely, consider an intensive lifestyle intervention focused on dietary change, physical activity, and weight loss such as 5 to 7 percent for benefits in quality of life, mobility, physical function, and cardiometabolic risk.
Select medications with low hypoglycemia risk for older adults with type 2 diabetes, especially when hypoglycemia risk factors are present.

For older adults at high hypoglycemia risk, deintensify insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides, or other hypoglycemia-causing medications, or switch to a lower-risk medication class, using individualized glycemic goals.
Deintensify diabetes medications in older adults when treatment harms or burdens may exceed benefits, within individualized glycemic goals.
Simplify complex diabetes treatment plans, especially insulin plans, to reduce hypoglycemia risk, polypharmacy, and treatment burden.

For older adults with type 2 diabetes and established or high risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease, include agents that reduce cardiovascular and kidney disease risk irrespective of glycemia.
Consider costs of care and coverage when developing treatment plans to reduce cost-related barriers to medication use and self-management.
Recommend diabetes education and training, including CGM, insulin pumps, and advanced insulin delivery systems, for staff in post-acute and long-term care settings.

For people with diabetes in post-acute and long-term care, assess mobility, mentation, medications, and management preferences to establish individualized glycemic goals and choose glucose-lowering agents and devices based on clinical and functional status.

When an older adult with diabetes needs palliative care, discuss goals and intensity of care with the person and care partners. Strict glucose, blood pressure, and lipid management are not necessary. Consider medication deintensification or simplification and prioritize symptom management.
At the end of life, prioritize comfort, prevention of distressing symptoms, quality of life, and dignity as the primary goals of diabetes management.
The ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes contains current clinical practice recommendations and is updated annually or more often when warranted by the ADA Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes.
This section directs readers to the separate Introduction and Methodology for the detailed evidence-grading system and full Professional Practice Committee information.
The American Geriatrics Society endorsed this section.
More than 29 percent of people older than 65 years have diabetes according to sources cited by the chapter.

Diabetes in older adults is heterogeneous across diabetes type, duration, complications, comorbidities, self-management capacity, support, treatment burden, hypoglycemia concerns, polypharmacy, and financial barriers.

Older adults with diabetes have higher rates of functional disability, accelerated muscle loss, mobility impairment, frailty, common geriatric syndromes, and several major comorbidities than older adults without diabetes, according to the chapter's cited evidence.
The chapter applies the age-friendly 4Ms framework to diabetes care: Mentation, Medications, Mobility, and What Matters Most.
Within the 4Ms framework, medication review includes hypoglycemia risk, treatment burden, affordability, end-organ disease, polypharmacy, adverse effects, and social or family support.
Within the 4Ms framework, mobility review includes foot problems, functional ability, frailty or sarcopenia, gait or dizziness, neuropathy, and sensory impairment.
Within the 4Ms framework, mentation review includes medication self-administration, ability to use diabetes technology, anxiety or depression, cognitive impairment, coping, and self-care.
The What Matters Most component asks about goals, symptom and disease burden, meal and treatment preferences, treatment risks and burdens, social isolation, quality of life, and life expectancy.
Table 13.1 pairs symptoms with screening approaches for geriatric syndromes and functional impairments and recommends using these tools when clinically indicated.
Table 13.1 lists Mini-Cog with a score below 3 as a validated dementia-screening cutoff and 4AT with a score of at least 4 as indicating possible delirium.
Table 13.1 lists a GDS-5 score of at least 2 as indicating possible depression and any yes response on the three-item STEADI screen as indicating increased fall risk.
Table 13.1 lists a Clinical Frailty Scale score of at least 5 as clinically meaningful frailty and SARC-F of at least 4 as indicating sarcopenia risk.
Table 13.1 lists Mini Nutritional Assessment Short Form scores of 12 to 14 as normal, 8 to 11 as at risk for malnutrition, and 0 to 7 as malnourished.

Table 13.1 lists Snellen visual acuity of 20/40 or worse as vision impairment, ISI-7 of at least 8 as insomnia, and Trail Making Test B completion time of at least 180 seconds as impaired executive function.
Older adults with diabetes are at higher risk of cognitive decline and institutionalization than older adults without diabetes, according to studies cited by the chapter.
The chapter reports higher incidence of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer disease, and vascular dementia among people with diabetes than among people without diabetes.
The chapter reports associations between both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia and cognitive decline, and between longer diabetes duration and worsening cognitive function.

When cognitive dysfunction is detected, the chapter advises simplifying care plans and engaging appropriate support because impaired cognition can disrupt glucose monitoring, insulin dosing, meal timing, and recognition or treatment of hypoglycemia.
Older adults have higher hypoglycemia risk because of factors that include erratic meal intake, insulin deficiency requiring insulin, and worsening kidney function.
Cognitive decline has been associated with increased hypoglycemia risk, while severe hypoglycemia has been linked to increased dementia risk in studies cited by the chapter.

The ORACL trial enrolled 30 older adults with type 1 diabetes, mean age 67 years, and found that automated insulin delivery improved time in range with modest improvement in hypoglycemia compared with sensor-augmented pump therapy.

canonical_statement: An open-label crossover trial in 37 adults aged at least 60 years found that 16 weeks of hybrid closed-loop therapy improved time in range and reduced time above range compared with sensor-augmented pump therapy, without a significant hypoglycemia difference.

canonical_statement: The ORACL and 37-participant crossover studies enrolled older adults whose baseline glycemia was relatively well managed, with mean A1C around 7.4 percent.

canonical_statement: A randomized trial in older adults with type 2 diabetes using multiple daily injections who could not manage insulin independently reported a 27 percent increase in time in range after 12 weeks of automated insulin delivery plus tailored home health care.

source_anchor.paragraph: Use of CGM and advanced insulin delivery devices

canonical_statement: The AIDE T1D study enrolled 82 adults at least 65 years old and reported less hypoglycemia with automated insulin delivery than with the comparison insulin-delivery approaches in its crossover design.

source_anchor.paragraph: Use of CGM and advanced insulin delivery devices

canonical_statement: In the AIDE T1D extension phase, 91 percent of participants chose the automated insulin delivery system.

canonical_statement: A real-world Medicare analysis of 4,243 people, 89 percent with type 1 diabetes and mean age 67.4 years, associated hybrid closed-loop initiation with improved mean glucose and a 10 percent increase in time in range.

canonical_statement: The chapter frames glycemic targets according to health status, life expectancy, cognitive and functional capacity, frailty, treatment burden, and risk of hypoglycemia rather than age alone.
Table 13.2 gives healthy older adults an A1C goal below 7.0 to 7.5 percent, fasting or preprandial glucose 80 to 130 mg/dL, bedtime glucose 80 to 180 mg/dL, and blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg.

Table 13.2 gives complex or intermediate older adults an A1C goal below 8.0 percent, fasting or preprandial glucose 90 to 150 mg/dL, bedtime glucose 100 to 180 mg/dL, and blood pressure below 130/80 mmHg.

Table 13.2 advises avoiding reliance on A1C in very complex or poor health and using glucose management to avoid hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia, with fasting or preprandial glucose 100 to 180 mg/dL, bedtime glucose 110 to 200 mg/dL, and blood pressure below 140/90 mmHg.

Table 13.2 recommends statin therapy for healthy and complex or intermediate older adults unless contraindicated or not tolerated, while very complex or poor health calls for considering the likelihood of statin benefit.
The chapter states that a lower A1C goal can be set if it can be achieved without recurrent or severe hypoglycemia or undue treatment burden.
For statins, the chapter cites an estimated time to benefit of 2.5 years and uses time to benefit as a consideration when deciding whether preventive therapy is likely to help an older adult.

The chapter links inadequate protein intake in older adults with loss of lean mass and recommends at least 0.8 g/kg/day, with individualized higher intake when needed to regain lean mass and function.
For sarcopenia and frailty, the chapter emphasizes exercise combined with adequate protein intake, including resistance or strength training, to preserve or improve function.
Look AHEAD enrolled adults aged 45 to 74 years who could perform a maximal exercise test and excluded people with low functional status, which limits direct application to frailer older adults.

Look AHEAD did not reduce its primary cardiovascular event outcome, but the intensive lifestyle intervention improved weight, physical fitness, HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure, A1C, waist circumference, and medication use, and age-stratified analyses showed similar benefits in participants aged 60 to 70 years.
The chapter states that overtreatment of diabetes is common in older adults and advises deintensification when treatment burdens or harms exceed expected benefits.
The chapter reports that deintensification protocols in diabetes and hypertension have been safe and possibly beneficial in older adults in cited studies.

Figure 13.2 begins by assessing treatment difficulty after medical or life-altering events, changes in physical, cognitive, or mental health, medication red flags, changed medication-taking behavior, unrecognized hypoglycemia, or hyperglycemia symptoms.
Figure 13.2 next reevaluates glycemic goals through shared decision-making with care partners.
Figure 13.2 then deintensifies, simplifies, or modifies treatment to improve safety, reduce polypharmacy, and target disease-specific benefits.
Figure 13.2 ends by reassessing treatment engagement and burden and suggests considering two weeks of CGM to evaluate glycemic patterns.

Metformin has low hypoglycemia risk and simple administration. The chapter permits its use at eGFR at least 30 mL/min/1.73 m2, recommends lower doses at eGFR 30 to 45, and advises monitoring eGFR every 3 to 6 months when kidney decline is a risk.

The chapter cautions against metformin in advanced kidney disease and in settings of hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, or impaired hepatic function because of lactic acidosis risk, and advises temporary interruption around some contrast procedures, hospitalizations, or acute illness that may compromise kidney or liver function.
Long-term metformin use beyond four years prompts annual vitamin B12 monitoring in the chapter.
Pioglitazone has low hypoglycemia risk but the chapter advises selective, cautious use because of heart failure, fluid retention, weight gain, osteoporosis, and macular edema risks.

Sulfonylureas and meglitinides increase hypoglycemia risk. The chapter prefers shorter-acting sulfonylureas when one is used and advises avoiding glyburide in older adults because it is longer acting, has active metabolites, and poses hypoglycemia risk.

The chapter notes that fluoroquinolones and sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim can interact with sulfonylureas and increase hypoglycemia risk, so sulfonylurea dose reduction or temporary discontinuation may be needed.

DPP-4 inhibitors have few side effects and minimal hypoglycemia risk but are relatively weak glucose-lowering agents and do not provide the cardiovascular or kidney risk reduction attributed to GLP-1 receptor agonists and SGLT2 inhibitors.
The chapter notes that linagliptin does not require renal dose adjustment and that DPP-4 inhibitors can be alternatives when low eGFR or intolerance limits other options.

The chapter reports that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death, stroke, and myocardial infarction to a similar degree in people above and below age 65 in a cited systematic review and meta-analysis.

The chapter cautions that GLP-1-based therapies require adequate visual, motor, and cognitive skills for most injectable formulations and may cause gastrointestinal adverse effects. It does not prefer them in older adults with unexplained weight loss, undernutrition, significant gastroparesis, recurrent ileus, bowel obstruction, or problematic constipation.

The chapter reports cardiovascular, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease benefits with SGLT2 inhibitors and states that trial stratification suggests similar or greater benefits in older adults than younger adults.

The chapter cautions that SGLT2 inhibitors can cause clinically significant volume depletion and genital mycotic infection, may slightly increase urinary tract infection risk, increase urine volume, and rarely cause euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis.
Once-daily basal insulin can be reasonable for many older adults, but the chapter prefers noninsulin therapies when feasible because of lower hypoglycemia risk and other potential benefits.
The chapter reports that long-acting insulin analogs were associated with fewer emergency department visits and hospitalizations for hypoglycemia than NPH insulin in a Medicare population.

Studies cited by the chapter associate insulin-plan simplification matched to self-management capacity and support with less hypoglycemia and diabetes-related distress without worsening glycemic outcomes.
For older adults with type 1 diabetes, basal insulin remains essential even when meals are not being consumed because stopping basal insulin can precipitate diabetic ketoacidosis.

canonical_statement: Figure 13.3 starts insulin simplification by optimizing technology use and caregiver engagement and then separates basal or prandial insulin plans from premixed insulin plans.

For basal insulin, Figure 13.3 moves dosing from bedtime to morning and titrates to a fasting glucose goal of 90 to 150 mg/dL, with at least a 2-unit increase when at least half of fasting values exceed goal and at least a 2-unit decrease when more than two fasting values per week are below 80 mg/dL.
For prandial insulin doses above 10 units per dose, Figure 13.3 reduces the dose by 50 percent, adds a noninsulin agent, and aims to discontinue prandial insulin as the noninsulin therapy increases.
For prandial insulin doses of 10 units or less per dose, Figure 13.3 discontinues prandial insulin and adds a noninsulin agent.

Figure 13.3 starts metformin 500 mg daily when eGFR is at least 45 mL/min/1.73 m2 and increases it every two weeks as tolerated, while directing lower-eGFR or metformin-intolerant patients to other agents based on comorbidities and complications.

Figure 13.3 gives an example simplified correction scale of 2 units of short- or rapid-acting insulin for premeal glucose above 250 mg/dL and 4 units for premeal glucose above 350 mg/dL, and says to stop the correction scale when it is no longer needed daily.

Table 13.3 defines treatment-plan simplification as reducing medication-plan complexity, administration times, glucose checks, or calculations, and defines deintensification or deprescribing as reducing dose or frequency or discontinuing treatment.

For otherwise healthy older adults, Table 13.3 identifies severe or recurrent hypoglycemia on insulin, wide glucose excursions, and cognitive or functional decline after acute illness as reasons to simplify treatment, and hypoglycemia, wide excursions, or polypharmacy as reasons to deintensify.

For complex or intermediate health, Table 13.3 identifies severe or recurrent hypoglycemia, difficulty managing insulin, or major social change as reasons to simplify, and hypoglycemia, wide glucose excursions, or polypharmacy as reasons to deintensify.

For very complex or poor health, Table 13.3 emphasizes avoiding hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia and supports simplification when injections or finger sticks are burdensome and deintensification when medications lack clear benefit or eating is inconsistent.

At the end of life, Table 13.3 supports treatment simplification for treatment-related pain or caregiver stress and deintensification when diabetes medications do not clearly improve symptoms or comfort.
The chapter says post-acute and long-term care facilities should have policies and procedures for prevention, recognition, and management of hypoglycemia and symptomatic hyperglycemia.

In post-acute and long-term care, irregular meals, undernutrition, diminished appetite, and swallowing impairment can complicate glucose-lowering therapy. The chapter allows immediate postmeal rapid-acting insulin in selected cases when dosing needs to reflect actual carbohydrate intake.

The chapter identifies post-acute and long-term care residents as especially vulnerable to hypoglycemia because of cognitive or renal impairment, impaired counter-regulation, hydration problems, variable intake, feeding assistance, polypharmacy, and slowed absorption.
The chapter cites a study of 65 residents in eight long-term care facilities in which CGM provided information on hypoglycemia and time in severe hyperglycemia.

canonical_statement: The chapter cites a randomized trial in post-acute and long-term care in which real-time CGM for up to 60 days was safe and effective for guiding insulin doses, with no differences from point-of-care blood glucose monitoring in time in range, time below range, or mean glucose.

canonical_statement: The chapter proposes immediate clinical notification for glucose below 70 mg/dL without delaying hypoglycemia treatment, and prompt notification for persistent or clinically significant hyperglycemia, including repeated values above 250 mg/dL or values consistently above 300 mg/dL over two consecutive days.
Palliative diabetes care aims to promote comfort, manage and prevent pain, hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, and dehydration, and preserve dignity and quality of life when life expectancy is limited.
The chapter reports that a multicenter trial found improved quality of life after statin withdrawal among people with diabetes receiving palliative care.

For palliative care, the chapter suggests glycemic goals that avoid glucose below 70 mg/dL and severe hyperglycemia above 250 mg/dL when symptom burden increases, while recognizing individual variation.

For a stable person at the end of life, the chapter proposes continuing the existing medication plan with emphasis on preventing hypoglycemia and dehydration-producing hyperglycemia and states that A1C monitoring has no role.

For a person with organ failure at the end of life, the chapter prioritizes preventing hypoglycemia and dehydration, allows insulin reduction with declining intake in type 1 diabetes but says insulin should not be stopped, and recommends reducing hypoglycemia-causing drugs in type 2 diabetes.

For a dying person with type 2 diabetes, the chapter states that discontinuing all diabetes medications may be reasonable when oral intake has ceased. For type 1 diabetes, it notes no consensus but states that a small amount of basal insulin may prevent acute hyperglycemic complications and symptom burden.
The chapter concludes that diabetes management at the end of life should be person centered and prioritize individualized goals, comfort, symptom management, quality of life, and dignity.
